parole.testo: From Spanish abacá, from the Tagalog name for the plant, abaka.

parole.significato: to fit out (originally to provide the fore- and aft- castles)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish adive, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic ذِئْب (ḏiʔb).
Borrowed from Spanish adobe. Doublet of toub.
Borrowed from Spanish aficionado. Doublet of affectionné.
Borrowed from Spanish alcázar, from Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr). Doublet of château.
Borrowed from Spanish alcoba or Portuguese alcova, from Arabic اَلْقُبَّة (al-qubba, “vault, chamber with vaulted roof”).
Borrowed from Spanish alazán, from Andalusian Arabic اَلْأَصْهَب, from Classical Arabic أَصْهَب (ʔaṣhab).
Borrowed from Spanish alguazil (now alguacil), from Arabic اَلْوَزِير (al-wazīr, “minister, vizier”).
Borrowed from Spanish alpaca, from Aymara allpaqa.
Introduced into French from settlers visiting the Indies; from Spanish ananás, from Portuguese ananás, from Old Tupi naná (“pineapple”).

parole.significato: Andalusian (of, from or relating to the autonomous community of Andalusia, Spain)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish andaluz. The singular in -ou is probably a backformation from the plural. It became common first in the equestrian sense, where the feminine is rare; this then caused the spelling inconsistency between masculine and feminine forms (compare also absous, coi, esquimau, favori).

parole.significato: aporophobia (hatred of poverty or poor people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish aporofobia, from Ancient Greek ἄπορος (áporos, “indigent, poor”) + -fobia. Term coined by the Spanish philosopher Adela Cortina in the 1990s.
Borrowed from Spanish armada. Doublet of armée.
Borrowed from Spanish armadillo (“armadillo”) and armadilla (“small naval armada”), with the sense of "woodlouse" being a semantic loan from taxonomic name Armadillo (“genus of isopods”).
Borrowed from Spanish arroba, an old-fashioned weight unit.
Borrowed from Spanish arracacha, from Quechua raqacha.
Borrowed from Spanish arroba, an old weight unit.

parole.significato: to be experienced, to have experience with age
parole.testo: Calque of Spanish tener la botella. This term allegedly derived from a practice in which Romans would drink some of a bottle of wine on their birthday, storing away the rest. Thus the reference to age.

parole.significato: the azarole, fruit of the azérolier

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish acederaque, from Arabic أَزَادَرْخَت (ʔazādarḵat), from Persian آزاددرخت (âzâd-deraxt, from آزاد (âzâd, “noble”) + درخت (deraxt, “tree”), literally “noble tree”).

parole.significato: bagasse (residue from processing sugar cane after extracting the juice)
parole.testo: Attested since the 1720s, from Spanish bagazo, from baga (“berry”).

parole.significato: a piece of fabric, particularly wool
parole.testo: From Spanish bernia, possibly as a shortening from Latin Hibernia (“Ireland”) where this fabric was made.
Borrowed from Spanish bibliodiversidad (1990s). By surface analysis, biblio- + diversité.

parole.significato: bolívar (the currency of Venezuela, divided into 100 céntimos)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bolívar. Named after Venezuelan statesman and military officer Simón Bolívar (1783–1830).

From Spanish buscar, from Old Spanish buscar, boscar (“to seek, collect wood”), from Vulgar Latin *buscum (“wood”), from Frankish *busk (“wood”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“wood, bush”). Doublet of bois and bûche.

parole.significato: to coast, to hug the coastline (to travel by the coast)
parole.testo: Uncertain, perhaps from cap + -oter, influenced by Spanish cabo (“cape”). Borrowed from Spanish cacahuete, from cacahuate (“peanut”), from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl (“cocoa bean”).
Borrowed from Spanish cacao, ultimately from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl.
From Spanish cálao, from Tagalog kalaw.

From Spanish camarada, itself from cámara (“chamber”) rather than Italian camerata which is slightly later but which influenced the form camerade which is attested in the 16th and 17th centuries. Borrowed from Spanish canario (“canary, resident or native of the Canary Islands”).

parole.significato: the practice of cannibalism, eating another of one's own species

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish cauchuc (an early variant of caucho), from Quechua kawchu. The final -c was formerly variably pronounced or silent, but is now always silent.
Cognate with or borrowed from Spanish caparazón. Possibly related to carapace (with metathesis) + the suffix -on.
Borrowed from Spanish caracol, of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Spanish caramelo, derived from Portuguese caramelo, probably derived from Late Latin calamellus, and therefore doublet of the inherited chalumeau.
Borrowed from Spanish carapacho (“carapace, shell”), of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Middle French Castelan, borrowed from Spanish castellano, from Latin castellanus. Doublet of châtelain, the native French word, and castellan.
Probably a borrowing from Spanish casuista.

parole.significato: Catalan, Catalonian (native or inhabitant of Catalonia, Spain) (usually male)
Catalan, Catalonian (of, from or relating to Catalonia, Spain)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish caudillo, from Late Latin capitellum. Doublet of cadeau, cadet, and chapiteau.
Borrowed from Spanish cebiche, of uncertain origin; see that entry for more. Cf. escabèche.

parole.significato: a mixture of coffee and wine (or other alcohol)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish chicha, from Kuna chichab (“corn”).
From the brand name, ultimately from Spanish chicle, from Classical Nahuatl tzictli.
Borrowed from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl, of uncertain origin; see that entry for more information.

parole.significato: cigar (rolled bundle of tobacco made for smoking)
a football match between Olympique de Marseille and Paris Saint-Germain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish clásico (“classic; match between rivals”). Doublet of classique.

Inherited from Middle French cochenille, cossenille, probably borrowed from Spanish cochinilla, itself probably a diminutive of cochino. From Spanish comprar (“to buy”) + chico (“kid”), coined by Victor Hugo in 1869.
From Spanish copal, from Classical Nahuatl copalli (“incense”).
Borrowed from Spanish coyote, from a Nahuan language, from Proto-Nahuan *koyoo-tl.

An adaptation of the Castilian Spanish criollo (“homey, local yokel”), from Portuguese crioulo, diminutive of cria (“person raised in one’s house, servant”), from Portuguese criar (“to rear, to bring up”), from Latin creō (“to create”)

Borrowed, through Italian, from Spanish dorada. Doublet of dorée.

parole.significato: a Spanish coin worth five pesetas

parole.testo: From Dulcinée, calque of the Spanish Dulcinea, a character from Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes.

parole.significato: to clear (a table, a desk etc.)
escabeche (a dish of fried fish, or other food, marinated in vinegar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish escabeche, which see for more.
Inherited from Middle French esquiver (“to escape”), from Spanish esquivar (“to avoid, reject, elude”), itself from Old French eschiver from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhan, if not formed from esquivo.

parole.significato: the mortal impalement of a bull
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French estoquade. Borrowed from Spanish estocada, ultimately from Italian stoccata.
Borrowed from Spanish estrado, from Latin strātum. Doublet of stratum.

parole.significato: A falcata; an Iberian single-edged curved sword.
parole.testo: From Spanish falcata, from Latin falcātus.
Borrowed from Spanish fanfarrón; in turn perhaps related to Arabic فَرْفَار (farfār).

parole.significato: smug or proud of one's appearance or clothing

Borrowed from Spanish fiesta. Originally Parisian slang. Doublet of fête.
Derived from Spanish alfil, from Arabic اَلْفِيل (al-fīl, “elephant; bishop (chess piece)”), influenced by Etymology 1 in the sense of "court jester."

parole.significato: Fuegian (resident or native of Tierra del Fuego)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish gabardina (perhaps influenced by gabán (“overcoat”) and tabardina (“coarse coat”)), from Middle French galverdine, itself probably from (Old or Middle) High German wallevart (“pilgrimage”), in the sense of "pilgrim's cloak".
Borrowed from Spanish gamella, from Latin camella.
Borrowed from Spanish gitano, itself derived from apheresis of older egiptano (“Egyptian”), from the mistaken belief that gypsies originated from Egypt.

parole.significato: Something that is added, especially something that a merchant gives to a buyer to complete the amount requested, or som…
goal scorer; attacker (who scores many goals)

Borrowed from Spanish guano, from Quechua wanu.
Borrowed from Spanish hacienda. Doublet of fazenda.

parole.significato: a kind of card game from Spain

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish hablar. Doublet of fabuler.
Borrowed from Spanish iguana, from Taíno *iwana.

Rebracketing of l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from Latin ilia (“flank”) (jade was thought to cure pains in the side).

parole.significato: tip (extra money given to, for example, a waiter in appreciation of service)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish la ñapa, a variant of yapa, from Quechua yapa (“addition, increase supplement”), yapay (“addition; sum”).
From Spanish llama, from Quechua llama.
From lamenti, an alteration of Spanish manatí, a Cariban word, by association with lamenter (“lament, bewail”), because of the animal's cry.
Borrowed from Spanish lima, from Arabic لِيمَة (līma).
From Spanish listón. By surface analysis, liste + -on.

parole.significato: One who is excessively or aggressively masculine or misogynistic; a chauvinist
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish macho, from Latin masculus. Doublet of mâle. :* c. 1952 :* c. 1962

parole.significato: madrague (a large fish pound used for the capture of tuna in the Mediterranean, now a forbidden practice in places)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish almadraba, from Arabic مضربة (maḍraba), ضرب (ḍaraba). Attested since 1679.

parole.significato: the highest non-commissioned officer rank: sergeant major, “major”
parole.testo: From Middle French major, from Spanish mayor, from Latin maior. Doublet of maire, majeur, and mayeur. The use for a non-commissioned officer in the French army (since 1972) is a short form of adjudant-major or sergent-major.
Alteration of earlier malille, from Spanish malilla, diminutive of mala.

parole.significato: plant fibre similar to hemp, harvested in the Philippines

parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Spanish marear (“to get dizzy”), with semantic shift "to get dizzy" > "to be bored" > "to be amused" (via antiphrasis).

parole.significato: feral, maroon (that has become wild again (used of a slave or animal who has returned to a free or wild state))
parole.testo: From a West Indies creole, from Spanish cimarrón; see that entry for more.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: to ogle, to check out, to watch (e.g. an attractive person)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mate, from Quechua mati (“gourd”).
Borrowed from Spanish maíz, from Taíno mahís.
Borrowed from Spanish merengue, itself borrowed from French meringue.
Borrowed from Spanish mezcal, from Classical Nahuatl mexcalli.
Borrowed from Spanish moái, from Rapa Nui mo'ai (“statue, figurine”).

Borrowed from Spanish morrión, from morra (“upper part of the head”), from morro (“muzzle, snout”), from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”). Related to moraine (“an amassment of rocks on a glacier”) and morailles (“barnacle, twitch”).
From a European pidgin word spoken in Algeria, originally from Spanish mujer.

parole.significato: a boy serving on a ship: a cabin boy

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito, diminutive of mosca, from Latin musca, whence also the French doublet mouche (“a fly”). The metathesis of /k/ and /t/ might have been due to influence of tique (“a tick”).
Borrowed from Spanish mero. Ultimate origin obscure.
Borrowed from Spanish ñandú from Paraguayan Guarani ñandu guasu.

Borrowed from Spanish palabra, from Latin parabola. Doublet of parole and parabole.

parole.significato: flaunt, strut, show off (to display with ostentation)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish parangón, from Italian paragonare.

parole.significato: a female political activist, usually in a left-wing organization
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish pasionaria (“passionate one”), nickname (La Pasionaria) of Spanish anti-fascist activist Dolores Ibárruri (1895-1989)
Borrowed from Spanish pasodoble, from paso (“step”) + doble (“double”).

parole.significato: small roll of dough containing fragrant ingredients baked in order to perfume the air
parole.testo: From Spanish pastilla (“small roll of fragrant dough”), from Latin pastellum (“dough, paste”), a diminutive form of pasta (“dough, paste”). Doublet of pastel.
Borrowed from Spanish pecadillo, with change of gender.
Borrowed from Spanish, from the name of the city Pisco, from Quechua pishku, pisqu.

Borrowed from Spanish quinua, from Quechua kinwa.

parole.significato: the soft, mellow quality acquired by brandy as it is aged
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish rancio. Doublet of rance.

From saquer or its Spanish cognate sacar.
Borrowed from Spanish sainete, diminutive of saín.

parole.significato: siesta (a nap, especially an afternoon one taken during the hottest part of the day in some cultures)
a Spanish-American gold or silver coin, now the main currency unit of Peru (also new sol), or a coin of this value
parole.testo: From Spanish sol (“sun”), itself from Latin sol.
Borrowed from Spanish soldadesco, itself borrowed from Italian soldatesco. By surface analysis, soldat + -esque.

parole.significato: tobacco (any plant of the genus Nicotiana)

parole.testo: taco + français. From Spanish taco. From being a sandwich originating from the Lyon region made from taco bread, distinguishing it from the original Mexican taco and burrito.
Borrowed from Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl.

Inherited from Middle French toque, tocque (“toque", also "a type of hairstyle”), in some senses from Spanish toca (“headdress”) and in other senses from Italian tocca, from Lombard toh, from Lombardic *tuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk (“cloth”).

parole.significato: Pre-1990 spelling of toréro (“torero, bullfighter, toreador”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish toril. Related to taureau; for the suffix, compare chenil.

to fight a bull, in bullfighting

parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish trampolín or Italian trampolino. See also French tremplin.

parole.significato: to move livestock according to transhumance
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish trashumar, derived Latin trāns (“across, beyond”) + humus (“ground”).
Borrowed from Spanish vigía, itself a borrowing from Portuguese vigia, from vigiar. Cognate with French veille.
Borrowed from Spanish vicuña, from Quechua wik'uña.
From Spanish Xeres, obsolete spelling of the name of the Spanish city Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, where the beverage was produced.

parole.testo: From Spanish español or from Middle French espaignol, from Old French espagneul or espaigneul, borrowed from Old Occitan espaignol, espainol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispaniolus, from Latin Hispānus, from Hispania. Doublet of épagneul and Pagnol.
